package_info.package_manager: N/A (malware binary, not a package manager ecosystem)
package_info.why_malicious: Abyss Locker is a ransomware family that encrypts user files, exfiltrates sensitive data, deletes backups and shadow copies, and demands ransom for decryption and non-disclosure. It disrupts business operations, threatens data privacy, and causes financial and reputational harm.

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: Stops critical services (e.g., SQLAgent$MSFW, WinDefend, MSExchangeIS, ShadowProtectSvc, IISADMIN, QuickBooksDB1, DefWatch, veeam, backup, etc.)
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, the code enumerates and forcibly stops a wide range of services related to databases, backups, security, and business applications, preventing them from interfering with the ransomware's file encryption process.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Stopping security, backup, and database services is a common tactic to maximize ransomware impact and prevent recovery.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate software should not indiscriminately terminate critical business and security services.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Maintenance scripts may stop specific services for upgrades, but not at this scale or with this intent.
key_indicators: Targeting backup, security, and database services

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: Terminates processes: ProcessHacker.exe, Procexp.exe, MsMpEng.exe, Sysmon.exe, TeamViewer.exe, etc.
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, the code enumerates and forcibly kills processes associated with security tools, monitoring, remote access, and productivity applications to evade detection and maximize file encryption coverage.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Killing security and monitoring processes is a hallmark of ransomware and other evasive malware.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normal applications do not terminate unrelated security or productivity processes.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Rarely, uninstallers may kill their own processes, but not third-party security tools.

malicious_snippets.code_snippet:
vssadmin.exe delete shadows /all /quiet
wmic SHADOWCOPY DELETE
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, the code executes system commands to delete all Volume Shadow Copies, removing backup snapshots and making file recovery more difficult.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Deleting shadow copies is a classic ransomware anti-recovery technique.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate software should not delete all system backups without user consent.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Backup management tools may prune old snapshots, but not all at once and not silently.
key_indicators: Silent deletion of all shadow copies

malicious_snippets.code_snippet:
bcdedit /set {default} recoveryenabled No
bcdedit /set {default} bootstatuspolicy IgnoreAllFailures
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, the code disables Windows automatic repair and configures the system to ignore all boot failures, impeding recovery efforts after a ransomware attack.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Disabling recovery features is a deliberate anti-forensics and anti-recovery tactic.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normal software should not alter boot recovery settings without explicit administrative intent.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Advanced troubleshooting may require these commands, but not in normal operation.

execution_context.file_location: malware main binary (Windows and Linux variants)

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: Encrypts files, appends .abyss (v1 Windows), random 5-letter extension (v1 Windows), or .crypt (v2 Linux/Windows), skips certain extensions/folders/files.
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, the code recursively encrypts user and business files, appending a unique extension, while skipping system-critical files, certain extensions, and whitelisted directories to ensure system stability and maximize ransom leverage.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Mass file encryption with ransom note drop is the core behavior of ransomware.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate software does not encrypt user files en masse without user consent.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Encryption tools may encrypt files, but only with user initiation and clear intent.

execution_context.file_location: malware main binary (Linux variant, ESXi environments)

malicious_snippets.code_snippet:
esxcli vm process list
esxcli vm process kill -t=soft -w=[ID]
esxcli vm process kill -t=hard -w=[ID]
esxcli vm process kill -t=force -w=[ID]
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, the code enumerates and attempts to gracefully, then forcefully, terminate running virtual machines on ESXi hosts to ensure files are not locked and can be encrypted.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Targeting and killing VMs is a tactic to maximize ransomware impact in virtualized environments.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate VM management does not indiscriminately kill all VMs without user approval.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: VM administrators may kill stuck VMs, but not all at once and not for malicious purposes.
key_indicators: Use of ESXi management commands in malware

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: Drops ransom note (WhatHappened.txt or .README_TO_RESTORE) and replaces desktop wallpaper with ransom message.
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, the code creates ransom note files and modifies the desktop wallpaper to display ransom instructions, coercing the victim to pay for decryption.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Dropping ransom notes and altering user interface is a direct indicator of ransomware.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate software does not extort users or alter their desktop environment for ransom.

attack_chain.action: Terminate critical services and processes to disable security, backup, and productivity tools.
attack_chain.leads_to: Prepares the environment for successful file encryption and anti-recovery.

attack_chain.action: Delete Volume Shadow Copies and system backups to prevent file recovery.
attack_chain.leads_to: Ensures that victims cannot restore files from backups.

attack_chain.action: Disable Windows recovery and repair features to impede system restoration.
Terminate running virtual machines (Linux/ESXi variant) to unlock files for encryption.
attack_chain.leads_to: Maximizes file encryption coverage in virtualized environments.

attack_chain.action: Recursively encrypt user and business files, appending unique extensions and skipping whitelisted files/folders.
attack_chain.leads_to: Denies access to critical data, setting up ransom demand.

attack_chain.action: Drop ransom note and modify desktop wallpaper to display ransom instructions.
attack_chain.leads_to: Coerces victim into ransom negotiation and payment.

behavioral_signatures: Mass termination of backup, security, and productivity services/processes
Execution of vssadmin.exe or wmic SHADOWCOPY DELETE
Modification of boot recovery settings via bcdedit
Recursive file encryption with new extensions (.abyss, .crypt, random 5-letter)
Creation of ransom note files and desktop wallpaper changes
ESXi VM process enumeration and termination
file_indicators: Desktop wallpaper image replaced with ransom message
network_indicators: Outbound connections to TOR negotiation sites (as referenced in ransom notes)
Potential exfiltration of stolen data prior to encryption (not directly shown in code, but described in behavior)
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor for mass service/process termination events, especially targeting backup, security, and productivity tools. Alert on execution of vssadmin.exe or wmic SHADOWCOPY DELETE commands. Detect changes to boot recovery settings via bcdedit. Flag recursive file encryption with new or unusual extensions and the sudden appearance of ransom note files. In ESXi environments, monitor for mass VM termination via esxcli. Correlate with outbound TOR traffic and potential data exfiltration events.
